screens.title: Advanced Animation Techniques
screens.subtitle: Blend Trees, IK, Layers, scripting and events for responsive characters

narration.text: In this lesson we explore the animation tools you will use to make characters feel responsive and believable. You will learn how Blend Trees let one or two parameters smoothly mix multiple clips so movement flows without abrupt cuts. You will also see how inverse kinematics lets a hand or foot reach a precise world position, and how layers and avatar masks let different parts of a body play different animations at once. Finally, we cover scripting controls and animation events so animation can drive gameplay and vice versa. For example, a 1D Blend Tree driven by a Speed parameter will move a character from idle to walk to run in a continuous way, while an upper-body layer with an avatar mask will let the character aim without interrupting leg motion. Practically, these techniques reduce visual popping, increase realism, and make game logic easier to synchronize with motion. As you move through the screens, notice common pitfalls like incorrect mask ranges or zeroed IK weights, and practice the hands-on steps to build confidence. Which single technique will you try first to improve a character in your project?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Advanced animation techniques let gameplay and animation work together: smooth movement, accurate interaction, layered control, and frame-accurate game events.

screens.title: What you'll be able to do
screens.subtitle: Skill-based outcomes for animation control and integration

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to design parameter-driven blends, apply inverse kinematics to position a limb at runtime, and structure animation layers so different body regions animate independently. You will also script Animator parameters and states to react to gameplay signals, and place animation events to trigger sound or gameplay logic precisely. For example, you will create a 1D Blend Tree that moves a character from idle to running based on a Speed float, then implement OnAnimatorIK to make a right hand reach a dynamic target. These skills matter because they connect animation to player input and game systems, reducing visual popping and improving responsiveness. A common misconception is that animation must be purely authored; in practice, runtime control produces far richer interactions. Each objective is paired with a small milestone that proves competency, from creating a Blend Tree to firing a frame-accurate event. As you progress, you'll verify these milestones and gain practical confidence integrating animation into gameplay.

narration.text: This screen describes measurable checks and common pitfalls to help you verify each objective. For Blend Trees, the milestone is a 1D tree that uses a Speed float to blend Idle, Walk, and Run without animation popping; verify by changing Speed in Play mode and watching the continuous interpolation. screens.title: Blend Trees — the definition
screens.subtitle: What a Blend Tree is and why it replaces abrupt transitions

narration.text: A Blend Tree is an Animator state that blends multiple animation clips based on one or more parameters. Instead of hard state-to-state transitions, a Blend Tree creates a continuous surface of motion where clips are interpolated depending on parameter values. For a concrete example, imagine a 1D Blend Tree that maps Speed equals zero to Idle, Speed equals two to Walk, and Speed equals five to Run. As your character's speed value moves from zero to five, Unity interpolates between the clips so the motion flows without sudden jumps. A common misconception is thinking Blend Trees remove the need for careful clip editing — they do not. You still need alignment between clips and matching root motion or poses at thresholds to avoid minor foot sliding. Another contrast: unlike manual cross-fades between states, a 2D Blend Tree can blend based on directional parameters, which is useful for combining forward and sideways movement. Key takeaway: Blend Trees convert discrete clips into a parametric continuum, which simplifies animator logic and produces smoother runtime motion. Try plotting simple thresholds and watching the parameter sweep to internalize how interpolation behaves.

keyIdea.title: Blend Tree essence
keyIdea.text: Blend Trees create a parametric continuous mix of animation clips, reducing popping and simplifying movement logic.

content.html:
Definition

Blend Tree

A state that blends multiple clips according to parameter values, producing smooth motion across a range.

Why it matters
  • Removes abrupt cuts between related motion clips.
  • Matches player-driven parameters like speed or direction.
  • Simplifies Animator graphs for movement systems.
Example
1D: Idle@0 → Walk@2 → Run@5 driven by Speed float.
Key Takeaway

Blend Trees map parameters to a smooth continuum of motion; align clips to avoid sliding.

Visual
1D Blend Graph
Parameter: Speed. Thresholds at 0, 2, 5. Unity interpolates clip weights automatically.
Common misconception
Blend Trees don't fix mismatched foot timing; synchronize gait cycles across clips before blending.
Try this
In Play mode, scrub Speed from 0 to 5 and watch the combined motion—adjust thresholds to tune transition feel.

screens.title: Creating a 1D Blend Tree in Unity
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step editor workflow and practical tips

narration.text: Creating a 1D Blend Tree in the Animator is procedural and repeatable. First, in the Animator window create a new state from a Blend Tree. Open the Blend Tree editor and set the Blend Type to 1D; create or select a float parameter such as Speed. Next, add motion slots and assign clips—place Idle at threshold 0, Walk at 2, Run at 5, or values that match your animations' perceived intensity. Unity will interpolate clip weights based on the Speed value. A concrete tip: place poses at similar points in the gait cycle across clips so feet align during blending. A common mistake is leaving thresholds inconsistent with the clip speeds; this yields odd pacing when the character transitions. After building, connect Entry to the Blend Tree state and remove redundant transitions to keep the graph tidy. In code, update the Speed parameter each frame using animator. SetFloat so runtime input drives the Blend Tree. Finally, test by changing Speed in Play mode and by using in-game velocity to verify the blend behaves correctly. Which threshold feels right depends on clip timing, so iterate and synchronize clips when necessary.

keyIdea.title: Blend Tree workflow
keyIdea.text: Create state → set 1D and parameter → add motion clips with thresholds → drive parameter from script.

content.html:
Process

Build a 1D Blend Tree

  1. Create State → From New Blend Tree, name it Movement.
  2. Set Blend Type to 1D and parameter to Speed (Float).
  3. Add motions: Idle (0), Walk (2), Run (5). Adjust thresholds to match clip pacing.
  4. Connect Entry and remove redundant transitions. Test by changing Speed at runtime.
Pro tip

Align gait cycles across clips and use root motion or matching locomotion speeds to reduce sliding when blending.

Example Code
// Pseudocode-style snippet for driving Speed
void Update() {
float inputSpeed = currentVelocity.magnitude;
animator.SetFloat("Speed", inputSpeed);
}
Testing: in Play mode,手 change the Speed parameter and watch the seamless interpolation between Idle, Walk, Run.

screens.title: 1D vs 2D Blend Trees
screens.subtitle: When to use one parameter or two for directional motion

narration.text: 1D and 2D Blend Trees serve similar goals but solve different problems. A 1D Blend Tree is ideal for a single continuum such as speed—idle to run is a classic case. A 2D Blend Tree gives you a two-parameter surface to blend, which is useful for movement that depends on forward/back and sideways input. For example, imagine a character that needs different clips for forward-walk, strafe-left, and strafe-right while also blending by forward speed; a 2D Freeform Directional or Freeform Cartesian blend lets you place those clips into a two-dimensional space driven by parameters like ForwardSpeed and SidewaysSpeed. Concretely, use a 1D blend when one variable determines motion intensity. Use 2D when direction and magnitude both change the resulting pose. A common misconception is that 2D always looks better; it can add complexity and require more clips and tuning. Also, a poorly sampled 2D space can create unexpected cross-blends. Key takeaway: pick the least complex tree that meets gameplay needs, and sample the parameter space with representative clips to avoid holes in motion coverage. 1D vs 2D Blend Trees means use 1d for single-parameter intensity changes and 2d for directional or multi-parameter motion control.. In practical terms, when to use one parameter or two for directional motion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choosing the right tree
keyIdea.text: Use 1D for single-parameter intensity changes and 2D for directional or multi-parameter motion control.

content.html:
Comparison
1D Blend Tree
Parameter: Speed. Good for idle→walk→run. Fewer clips, simpler thresholds.
2D Blend Tree
Parameters: ForwardSpeed + SidewaysSpeed. Good for directional blends like strafing and diagonal motion.
Example: A top-down shooter might use 2D blending to combine aim direction and movement speed so animations match both direction and speed.
Pitfall
Overcomplicating a tree adds tuning cost and runtime weight; prefer 1D unless direction matters.
Key Takeaway

Match tree dimensionality to gameplay requirements and sample the space with representative clips.

screens.title: Inverse Kinematics (IK) Fundamentals
screens.subtitle: How IK differs from forward kinematics and what problems it solves

narration.text: Inverse Kinematics reverses the usual forward calculation: instead of computing an end effector position from joint rotations, you specify the desired end effector position and let the solver compute necessary joint rotations. Practically, that means you can ask a character's hand to touch a door handle or a foot to plant on uneven ground without authoring many bespoke clips. A concrete example: in a pickup animation you place an IK target on the object and the hand will reach the object's transform; using SetIKPosition and SetIKRotation you can control both placement and orientation. A common misconception is that IK will always produce perfect anatomical motion — it can look mechanical if joint limits, weights, or pole vectors are not tuned. Also, performance cost matters: running full IK on many characters every frame can be expensive. Key takeaway: use IK when interaction accuracy matters and keep weight tuning and performance in mind. When you implement IK, always provide fallbacks and zeroed weights so the system can be disabled gracefully. Inverse Kinematics (IK) Fundamentals means ik computes joint rotations from an end-target, enabling runtime-accurate placement of hands and feet for interaction.. In practical terms, how ik differs from forward kinematics and what problems it solves. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: IK in a sentence
keyIdea.text: IK computes joint rotations from an end-target, enabling runtime-accurate placement of hands and feet for interaction.

content.html:
Definition

Inverse Kinematics (IK)

Specify an end effector position and let the solver calculate intermediate joint rotations to reach that point.

Example: animator.SetIKPosition(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, target.position) and set the IK weights to control influence.
Notes
  • Tune position and rotation weights so IK blends naturally with authored animation.
  • Use pole vectors or additional constraints to avoid unnatural elbow or knee twisting.
  • Disable or reduce IK on distant characters to save CPU.
Misconception: IK is a magic fix for bad animation. It helps placement but does not replace good posing and joint limit setup.

screens.title: Implementing OnAnimatorIK
screens.subtitle: A guided walkthrough of the OnAnimatorIK callback and key API calls

narration.text: OnAnimatorIK is a Unity callback that runs during the animation update, allowing you to set IK targets and weights before the frame renders. In practice, you implement OnAnimatorIK on a MonoBehaviour with a reference to the Animator and an optional target Transform. Inside the method, check that the animator exists and then call SetIKPositionWeight and SetIKRotationWeight to control the solver's influence. Then call SetIKPosition and SetIKRotation with the target's position and rotation. A concrete example is making a right hand reach a pickable object: assign an IKTarget transform to the hand reference and in OnAnimatorIK set full weights when the interaction is active. A common mistake is forgetting to set weights, which makes SetIKPosition appear to do nothing. Another is manipulating IK outside of OnAnimatorIK, which can cause timing issues. Performance note: call these methods only when needed and consider reducing weight updates on distant actors. When you test, move the IK target in the Scene view and watch the hand follow in Play mode to confirm the connection. Implementing OnAnimatorIK means set weights then positions inside onanimatorik; always handle null targets and provide zero-weight fallback.. In practical terms, a guided walkthrough of the onanimatorik callback and key api calls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: IK implementation tip
keyIdea.text: Set weights then positions inside OnAnimatorIK; always handle null targets and provide zero-weight fallback.

content.html:
Code
void OnAnimatorIK(int layerIndex) {
if (animator) {
if (ikTarget != null) {
animator.SetIKPositionWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, 1f);
animator.SetIKRotationWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, 1f);
animator.SetIKPosition(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, ikTarget.position);
animator.SetIKRotation(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, ikTarget.rotation);
} else {
animator.SetIKPositionWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, 0f);
animator.SetIKRotationWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, 0f);
}
}
}
Keep weight changes explicit and avoid toggling IK mid-blend without smoothing to prevent pops.
Explanation
  • Set position and rotation weights before calling SetIKPosition/Rotation.
  • Provide default zero weights when no target exists to avoid residual influence.
  • Use smoothing functions like Mathf.Lerp on weights to blend IK in and out.
Check your understanding

What happens if you set positions but leave weights at zero? Try it and observe that the solver has no effect.

screens.title: Animation Layers and Avatar Masks
screens.subtitle: Separating upper- and lower-body motion with weights and masks

narration.text: Animation Layers allow different sets of animations to run in parallel with configurable influence, and Avatar Masks define which bones a layer controls. For example, you can keep a base layer for locomotion and add an upper-body layer for aiming or gestures. Set the upper-body layer's Avatar Mask to include arms and chest only, so legs remain animated by the base layer. Layer weight controls how much the layer overrides lower layers; a weight of one fully applies the upper-body animation, while lower values blend between layer animations. A common pitfall is mis-configured masks that omit critical bones or include unintended ones, which produces visible artifacts. Always inspect your Avatar Mask to visualize the covered bones and test with a blend value to confirm the result. Another important point: layer blending is evaluated per-frame, so adjusting weights at runtime allows dynamic transitions such as smoothly engaging aim over time. Key takeaway: layers plus masks let you compose complex actions like walking while shooting without authoring a combinatorial set of full-body clips. Animation Layers and Avatar Masks means use layers to overlay actions and avatar masks to restrict animation influence to selected bones for composable motion.. In practical terms, separating upper- and lower-body motion with weights and masks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Layering principle
keyIdea.text: Use layers to overlay actions and avatar masks to restrict animation influence to selected bones for composable motion.

content.html:
Definition

Animation Layers

Parallel animation tracks with weights that blend and override lower layers for specified bones via Avatar Masks.

Example: base locomotion layer + upper-body layer with avatar mask affects only arms and torso so aiming animation does not stop walking.
Practical tips
  • Always preview Avatar Masks in the Inspector to confirm bone selection.
  • Use layer weights to smoothly blend an action in and out, avoiding pops.
  • Keep layer graphs limited to necessary actions to reduce runtime overhead.
Mistake: setting weight to 1 but forgetting to mask out lower-body bones, leading to conflicting motion between layers.

screens.title: Scripting Animator Control
screens.subtitle: Programmatic control: SetFloat, Play, and CrossFade for runtime behavior

narration.text: Scripting the Animator gives you direct control over parameters, states, and transitions. Use animator. SetFloat to feed parameters used by Blend Trees, animator. SetBool and SetTrigger for state logic, and animator. Play or animator. CrossFade to immediately start or smoothly blend into a named state. For instance, calling animator. CrossFade("Reload", 0.2f) blends into the reload animation over two tenths of a second, which can be preferable to an abrupt animator. Play. A concrete example from the hands-on: update Speed each frame using inputs or velocity so the Blend Tree responds to player movement. Be mindful that animator. Play bypasses transitions and can interrupt current blending, so prefer CrossFade when you want controlled blends. Another misconception is that Play is always cheaper—Play can cause visual discontinuities. Also avoid calling state transitions every frame unnecessarily; set parameters and let the Animator evaluate the graph. Key takeaway: use parameter APIs for continuous control and Play/CrossFade selectively for direct state changes, balancing responsiveness with visual continuity. Scripting Animator Control means drive blend parameters continuously, prefer crossfade for smooth state changes, and avoid forcing play every frame to prevent visual jumps.. In practical terms, programmatic control: setfloat, play, and crossfade for runtime behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Script control rules
keyIdea.text: Drive blend parameters continuously, prefer CrossFade for smooth state changes, and avoid forcing Play every frame to prevent visual jumps.

content.html:
Architecture

Animator Scripting Patterns

Use SetFloat("Speed", value) to drive Blend Trees.
Use CrossFade("State", 0.2f) to transition smoothly to a named state.
Use Play for immediate, non-blended state switching when intentional.
Example
// Drive Blend Tree
float speed = rb.velocity.magnitude;
animator.SetFloat("Speed", speed);
// Smoothly start reload
animator.CrossFade("Reload", 0.2f);
Design rule: update parameter values from your movement system, not every UI event, to preserve consistent animation logic.

screens.title: Animation Events
screens.subtitle: Synchronize gameplay and audio with frame-accurate markers

narration.text: Animation Events are markers you place on an animation clip's timeline that call a public method on scripts attached to the same GameObject when the timeline reaches that frame. They are straightforward to use: open the Animation window, move the playhead to the desired frame, click Add Event, and choose a public method from the Inspector. A common use is playing a footstep sound exactly when a foot contacts the ground, or spawning particles at the peak of a swing. A concrete example: add an event to call PlayFootstep() in your audio script at the frame where the foot hits. Misconceptions include thinking events can call private methods or pass arbitrary complex arguments; they require a public method signature and support only limited parameter types provided by the event UI. Also, avoid placing heavy C P U work directly in an event handler; instead, trigger lightweight flags or enqueue work to other systems. Key takeaway: animation events are the simplest way to synchronize logic with motion, but use them judiciously and keep handlers efficient. Animation Events means use events to trigger light-weight, frame-accurate actions and avoid heavy processing inside event callbacks.. In practical terms, synchronize gameplay and audio with frame-accurate markers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event best practice
keyIdea.text: Use events to trigger light-weight, frame-accurate actions and avoid heavy processing inside event callbacks.

content.html:
Definition

Animation Events

Timeline markers that call a public method when the animation reaches the frame, perfect for synchronized audio or particle triggers.

Example: Add event to call PlayFootstep() on the frame where the foot contacts the ground to align sound precisely.
Practical note
  • Events require a public method on the same GameObject for simple calls.
  • Only pass supported parameter types; prefer no-argument calls when in doubt.
  • Keep handlers light; set flags or call audio managers rather than heavy logic directly.
Key Takeaway

Events give precise synchronization between motion and gameplay; use them for timing, not heavy processing.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Performance Considerations
screens.subtitle: What to profile and how to avoid costly animation setups

narration.text: Advanced animation systems can strain performance or produce visible errors if not configured carefully. A frequent mistake is overusing IK on many actors at full weight every frame; your solver cost grows with each affected character. Another is incorrect avatar masks that either overreach and cause conflicting motion or under-include bones leading to missing animation. Clip mismatch across Blend Trees causes foot sliding and awkward pacing when thresholds don't align with gait cycles. To test performance, use the Profiler to isolate animation update costs and disable expensive systems on distant characters. A practical optimization is to reduce IK frequency or lower weight for distant actors, and to use simplified blends or fewer clips for far LODs. Also, avoid calling animator. Play repeatedly in Update; instead set parameters or call CrossFade with sensible durations. Key takeaway: test both correctness and cost; small visual fixes like mask tuning often solve apparent animation bugs, while profiling reveals where to reduce complexity for many characters. Common Mistakes and Performance Considerations means profile animation updates, limit heavy ik usage, and simplify blend trees for distant characters to maintain performance.. In practical terms, what to profile and how to avoid costly animation setups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Performance focus
keyIdea.text: Profile animation updates, limit heavy IK usage, and simplify Blend Trees for distant characters to maintain performance.

content.html:
Mistakes
  • Forgetting to set IK weights makes the solver appear inactive.
  • Incorrect avatar masks cause unintended overrides or missing joints.
  • Misaligned gait cycles produce foot sliding in Blend Trees.
Tip: verify masks and weights visually before profiling performance; many bugs are configuration errors.
Performance Checklist
Profile animation update cost in the Profiler.
Use lower-cost blends or fewer clips for distant LODs.
Limit IK passes per-frame or disable on non-interactive actors.
Avoid per-frame state forcing; prefer parameter updates and CrossFade.

screens.title: Lab: 1D Blend Tree + Basic Right-Hand IK
screens.subtitle: Step sequence to complete the guided exercise in your scene

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through building a 1D Blend Tree and a simple IK target for the right hand. Start by opening the PlayerAnimatorController and removing legacy Idle and Walk states if present. Create a new Blend Tree state named Movement, set its Blend Type to 1D, and create a Float parameter called Speed. Add three motions: Idle at 0, Walk at 2, Run at 5, and connect Entry to Movement. Next, in the scene create an empty GameObject named IKTarget and position it in front of the character's right hand. Add the provided PlayerAnimationHandler script to the character, assign the Animator and IKTarget references, and ensure the script updates moveSpeed from input or a simulated variable. Finally, implement OnAnimatorIK as in the example and test in Play mode: press your movement key to change Speed and drag IKTarget in the Scene view to confirm the right hand reaches it. Watch for issues: if the hand doesn't follow, check that IKPositionWeight is set to one and that the Animator has Apply Avatar IK enabled. This lab verifies both Blend Tree blending and IK integration in a single character.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: A functioning 1D Movement Blend Tree and an IK target that the right hand reaches, confirming runtime integration.

content.html:
Step-by-step
  1. Create Movement Blend Tree (1D) and Speed parameter.
  2. Add Idle@0, Walk@2, Run@5 motions and connect Entry.
  3. Create IKTarget GameObject and assign to script.
  4. Attach PlayerAnimationHandler, set ikTarget, and enable Apply Avatar IK in Animator.
  5. Run scene, press movement keys, and move IKTarget to observe hand tracking.
Debug checklist

If IK doesn't move the hand, confirm IK weights are set and that animator.SetFloat("Speed") is updating the parameter.

Starter script (summary)
public class PlayerAnimationHandler : MonoBehaviour {
Animator animator; public Transform ikTarget; float moveSpeed;
void Update(){ animator.SetFloat("Speed", moveSpeed); }
void OnAnimatorIK(int layerIndex){ /* set weights and positions as needed */ }
}
Run the scene and iteratively tune thresholds, IK weights, and mask coverage until motion looks natural.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to take forward

narration.text: These are the essential ideas to keep in mind as you apply advanced animation techniques. First, Blend Trees turn discrete clips into smooth, parameter-driven motion; pick 1D when a single intensity parameter like speed suffices, and 2D when direction plus magnitude affect the pose. Second, Inverse Kinematics allows precise end-effector placement but requires weight tuning and constraint care; always set weights and test fallbacks. Third, Animation Layers combined with Avatar Masks let you compose independent body actions, so aim or gesture animations can overlay locomotion. Use CrossFade and parameter APIs for smooth scripted control, and place Animation Events only for lightweight frame-tied logic such as sound or particle triggers. Finally, profile your animation costs and limit heavy IK usage on many simultaneous characters. Remember these three principles and you'll be able to design animations that respond to gameplay without unexpected visual artifacts.

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: Blend parametric motion, use IK with weight control, and compose actions with layers and masks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Key Concepts
Blend Trees
Parameter-driven blending that produces continuous motion across clips.
Inverse Kinematics
Place an end effector and let the solver compute joint rotations; tune weights carefully.
Layers & Masks
Compose independent actions by bone region and layer weight for simultaneous behaviors.
Summary: Choose the right blend dimensionality, use IK for precise placement, and compose actions with layers. Profile when scaling to many characters.

narration.text: Use this final screen as a quick reference when you return to your project. Blend Trees make parameter-driven motion simple and should be your first tool for locomotion blending. IK is perfect for runtime interactions but always set weights and provide fallback behavior when targets are missing. Animation Layers and Avatar Masks let you overlay actions like aiming or reloading without interrupting movement. When scripting Animator behavior, prefer parameter updates and CrossFade for smooth changes. Use Animation Events for frame-accurate triggers like footsteps or weapon flashes, but keep handlers lightweight. Finally, always profile and reduce IK or complex trees on non-essential actors to maintain performance. Keep these rules on hand as a checklist while building your system. What to Remember means blend trees → ik weights → layers & masks → script with crossfade → event handlers lightweight → profile.. In practical terms, three quick reference cards. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Quick Reference
Blend Trees
Map floats to continuous motion and align clip cycles for smooth blends.
IK
Always set weights and test with and without targets to ensure graceful fallback.
Layers & Events
Use avatar masks to limit influence and events for frame-accurate, lightweight actions.
Final takeaway

Combine these tools thoughtfully: smooth blends, precise IK, and layered composition let animation support gameplay without surprising behavior.
